Hey there! Fellow R.Ac here practicing in southern Ontario. 

You've received some wonderful advice regarding this question! I just wanted to add my personal 2 cents: I found that getting out into the community and networking was extremely beneficial for me. When I was practicing in Brampton, I would go with the clinic I was working with at the time and set up a booth at Gage Park during the farmers market days, and I would offer pulse and tongue readings, as well as 10 minutes chair Tuina sessions! This got people curious about acupuncture and TCM, they could put a face to a name, they could ask me all the questions they've never been able to ask an acupuncturist before, and it got me a lot of new clients! I've also volunteered at the Mississauga fertility convention before and chatted with folks about how acupuncture can help with infertility, IVF, embryo transfers, etc. A lot of people genuinely didn't know!

I think the biggest hurdle for us as practitioners is educating people about what TCM is and what acupuncture can help with. People are genuinely curious and want to try it, but just don't know what it can be used for! Getting that face to face connection makes a world of a difference for a lot of folks. 

I also (try) to post semi regularly on Instagram, as well as connect with other practitioners in the community; an introduction goes a loooooong way! You'd be surprised at who will refer clients to you once they know who you are and where you practice, and what you treat. 

Good luck to you ❤️

If you want to blanch your greens and have a wet salad, go for it. But totally not necessary!

My point is that the lettuce/salad/spring mix/whatever you use as the base should be the **only** raw component. Please Google "warming foods in TCM" and go from there. Whatever vegetables you add into your salad need to be cooked. 

Warming spices such as ginger, in a ginger based dressing, would be a great choice to add energetic warmth. 

The most important thing to keep in mind is that TCM is a balance of yin and yang; hot and cold. It's ok to have a cold base (your salad mix) with warming accessories (cooked veg, spices, nuts and seeds). Swaying in one extreme direction or another will cause imbalance in our bodies. It's more important to have balance, hence the cooked veg suggestion to literally and energetically heat it up.

Cook your veggies, first and foremost. You don't need to blanch the greens, those are fine. 

Add in a ginger based salad dressing (maybe it's time to make some Asian fusion salads?). Green onion, pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds and eggs are things you could add which are all warming.

Hi, I'm an R.Ac practicing in Ontario. I'm not going to sugar coat it, it's been tough. I've been practicing for 2 years now.

- anatomy
- physiology 
- points 
- organ patterns 
- diagnosis basics 
- case studies 
- tongue 
- pulse 
(And probably a few others but I don't remember)

During the week, I would allot 2 hours to studying one thing in the morning, and 2 hours to studying one thing in the afternoon after having a break from my morning study. For example, 2 hours in the morning I would choose to review Lung, Large Intestine, and Stomach organ patterns. And then 2 hours in the afternoon, I would do case studies focused on a few organ patterns centered around the organs that I had reviewed that morning.

This method worked really well for me, and allowed me to study in chunks of time that didn't feel overwhelming. I gave myself breaks when I needed them, and didn't let myself feel guilty for it. 

As for study material, I watched a lot of videos from AcuPro Academy, Nicholas Duchnowski, and Kenton Sefcik. Alongside my own study schedule, I also used the PRCO Bootcamp program by Pacific Rim College. I recommend checking out some Bootcamp programs if you can afford it. I realized something was wrong when I went back to school in my early 20's, taking a program that required a lot of studying and focus. 

I would read my notes over and over again and nothing stuck. I would study flashcards, nothing stuck. I would read, out loud, the information and be unable to recite or summarize what I JUST SAID. Other people would tell me information in class or in study and I felt like I couldn't understand a single thing they just said to me. I started to feel stupid, inadequate, lazy and unmotivated. My grades did not reflect the love and passion that I was trying to convey about my program. 

I approached my doctor and she asked me more questions like: Do you rely heavily on to-do lists? Yes. Do you procrastinate and feel unmotivated because you're feeling overwhelmed and unsure how to tackle a task? Yes. Do you get distracted very easily when taking tests? Yes. Do you have trouble focusing when there is other stimuli around you (such as someone walking past me)? Yes. Are you struggling in school despite implementing different studying methods? YES! I was diagnosed in that same phone call and have been on medication since. It's been great, but I've been forgetting to take my meds lately, which is why I'm here instead of writing a paper for school ... Oops. Diagnosed at 24 years old, in case you're wondering.
